title: Future loss of Arctic sea-ice cover could drive a substantial decrease in California’s rainfall
problem: Accurately projecting California's future rainfall is challenging because the physical mechanisms linking Arctic sea-ice loss to the formation of persistent, storm-blocking atmospheric ridges over the North Pacific are not fully understood.
method: To isolate the atmospheric impacts of Arctic sea-ice loss, the authors compare control climate model simulations with an ensemble of experiments where sea-ice physics parameters are perturbed in an energy-conserving framework to achieve a nearly ice-free Arctic condition.
task: The task is to identify and explain the physical mechanism by which future Arctic sea-ice loss could cause a substantial decrease in California's rainfall by using climate model simulations to demonstrate a two-step teleconnection involving changes in tropical convection.
innovation: This paper identifies a novel two-step teleconnection mechanism whereby Arctic sea-ice loss drives a reorganization of tropical convection, which in turn creates a persistent atmospheric ridge over the North Pacific that substantially reduces California's rainfall and exacerbates drought.

As in previous dry periods, precipitation-inducing winter storms were steered away from California by a persistent atmospheric ridging system in the North Pacific.

We conclude that sea-ice loss of the magnitude expected in the next decades could substantially impact California's precipitation, thus highlighting another mechanism by which human-caused climate change could exacerbate future California droughts.

From 2012 to 2016, California experienced one of the worst droughts since the start of observational records. As in previous dry periods, precipitation-inducing winter storms were steered away from California by a persistent atmospheric ridging system in the North Pacific.

These uncertainties are largely a consequence of the sensitivity of Californian rainfall to both tropical and mid-latitude atmospheric circulation changes, such as variability in the El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and shifts in the Pacific jet stream2–4.
A La Niña event in 2011/12 and anomalously warm sea-surface temperatures (SST) over the west tropical Pacific in 2012/13 and 2013/14 may have helped sustain the North Pacific geopotential ridge6, 8.

Another important factor may be the 2014 phase shift of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation from negative to positive. However, this shift would be expected to alleviate drought conditions over California—not intensify them42.

Data availability. Simulation output processed for the purpose of this study has been made public and can be obtained at https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/projects/psipps/ . Provided are monthly means of the following CAM4 variables: ice fraction (ICEFRAC), surface pressure (PS), surface temperature (TS), upper tropospheric temperature (TROP_T), total precipitation (PRECT), geopotential (Z3), horizontal and meridional wind speed components (U and V), vertical (pressure) velocity (OMEGA), net longwave flux at the atmosphere top (FLNT), and high cloud cover (CLDHGH); all for years 20-40 of model integration. Additional data can be made available on request.
